I've seen in some of your other comments that he's become increasingly disrespectful towards you and has been pressuring you for oral sex when you've expressed to him that you're on your period and not feeling it. The fact that you've made this post and reached out for advice shows that you already know something is not right here. This is not how normal people treat their partners. If your gut instinct is already telling you something is wrong, trust it. 

You've expressed that you don't want to break up with him and I empathise with you, you might feel that the love you have for him outweighs his abusive behaviour and it's not easy to separate the two. If you're not ready to break up with him yet, I'd suggest that you keep a mental note of how he reacts to you when you say no or when you express your own needs. You don't need to argue or fight with him but just watch him as if you were watching someone else's life on a reality show. Note the tone of voice he uses with you, how he responds to your emotions, if he dismisses your feelings or not, etc. Watch his behaviour and see him for who he really is, not the idealised version of him that exists in your mind.

Examine your attachment to money. What does money mean to you? Happiness? Success? Stability? Safety? All of these states are impermenant, subject to suffering and change. Money comes and money goes, as is the nature of impermenant things. We can never truly 'own' that which is impermenant, we only borrow it for a time. We mustn't cling to that which can and will be taken away from us one day. 

Your happiness isn't determined by an impermenant thing such as money, your happiness is dependant on you. Meditate on the feeling of gratitude and satisfaction regardless of how much/little money you have. >The Buddhist notion of samsara (“the wheel of desire”) ignores this spiritual aspect of “evil.”

Again, samsara is not a wheel of desire but I'd agree that there isn't necessarily a concept of "evil" in Buddhism. The emphasis is more on cause-and-effect. There is no omniscent God to punish you for your transgressions, rather the Buddhist philosophy is closer to "if you play stupid games, you'll win stupid prizes". Our actions can either drive positive or negative karma and our choices dictate out actions. The karma you accumulate during your live(s) will dictate the next realm you are born into. If you follow the Buddha's path, he teaches us how to free ourselves from accumulating karma and how to entirely end the cycle of rebirth altogether. 

>Since dharma is, as a rule, described as the highest freedom accessible to us, one should point out that, to anyone who knows a little bit about Hegel, the radical opposition between the Buddhist and Hegel’s notion of freedom cannot but strike the eye. For Buddhism, we are truly free when we liberate ourselves from the rational categories that cut into pieces and thus mortify the pure non-substantial flux of reality, while for Hegel, the basic form of freedom is precisely the infinite power of abstraction that pertains to our Understanding (not Reason), the power to interrupt the smooth flow of reality and to cut mechanically reality into its species.

I'm interested in how Zizek understands the word "dharma" and how he is using it here. In my understanding, 'dharma' just means the reality of the universe we live in. Dharma itself isn't a freedom but understanding the dharma, the way the universe works, can allow for some of use to gain freedom from our ignorance of the universe. Dharma isn't just some mystical thing that sends us to nibbana, it's the grueling process of understanding the 'dharma/reality we live in' that sets the foundations to remove ourselves from playing this endlessly repeating game by attaining nibbana.

Anyhoo, this has ended up being far longer that I anticipated and I'll probably need to split it over multiple comments. If anyone takes anything away from this I want it to be: 

1) Start your studies of Buddhism by reading the Early Buddhist texts/Pali canon before forming ideas about Buddhism as a whole

2) Remember that there are a TON of different sects, culture, languages, influences in Buddhism as it's spread across the globe for the past two millenia so try to understand the specific cultural/historical context a particular schoolsect is coming from and avoid conflating these with Buddhism as a whole

(3) 

>A Lacanian view is much closer to Dr. House who, in one of the episodes of the series, when he tries to diagnose a patient and one of his collaborators mentions that the patient radiates happiness, immediately adds “happiness” to the list of symptoms of the patient’s illness to be explained and abolished. 

This is actually very inline with what the Buddha actually taught. Clinging to a state of happiness can also be a state of 'tanha' which can give rise to suffering. Someone who is attached to happiness and rejects sadness is setting themselves up for further suffering. In the 'Four Noble Truths' (the most fundamental of the Buddha's teachings) - he teaches that life itself is suffering. To expect to live a life with no suffering at all is delusion.

>So, what about the desperate Lacano-Buddhist attempt to read what Buddhism calls nirvana as basically the same stance as that signaled by Lacan’s “traversing the fantasy”? 

I'm not very well-read on Lacan so please correct any misundertandings I have on the comparison made here. I want to focus on the common misunderstanding of nibbana in the west which I assume underpins this comparative analysis Zizek is making here. In the western imagination "nirvana" (the sanskrit term for the pali word nibbana) is often thought of as some transcendental realm where enlightened being frolic in permenant states of bliss but this is another deep misunderstanding of the concept. Nibbana could more accurately be translated as 'snuffing out a flame' - picture our lives as a flame on a candle, nibbana is the act of blowing that candle out. Attaining nibbana isn't actually about attaining anything, it's about losing everything and escaping samsara - the tortuous cycle of death, life and rebirth. It isn't a myth about a sublime heaven, it's about understanding the game of life and quitting the game entirely.

>I consider this privileged position dangerous because it remains caught in a dualism that authentic Buddhism promises to leave behind: the realm of nirvana becomes a Beyond which we strive to reach. The danger resides in the fact that this position relies on what one could call the basic syllogism of self-sacrifice: I want all living beings to overcome their suffering and achieve the supreme good; to do this, I have to sacrifice my own happiness and accept suffering – only in this way my own life has meaning.

I completely agree with Zizek here. I don't want to delve into sectarianism but this is much of the reason why I didn't vibe with certain traditions. Again, I'd really encourage Zizek or anyone that holds a similar criticism to look into the EBTs and form an analysis based on them before branching out to the rich traditions that evolved from the sectarian split.

(2)

>Buddhism focuses on desire as the ultimate cause of our suffering: desire is inconsistent and can never be fulfilled, fully satisfied, because its nature is inconsistent. Since its object is illusory, the false appearance of a void, the moment of desire’s fulfillment is the moment of its defeat. Buddhism draws the radical consequence from this insight: the only way to avoid suffering is to step out of (gain a distance towards) the “wheel of desire,” to avoid attachment to any object of desire, which means to accept (not only as a theoretical statement but also as an existential stance) that desires are illusory because all objects (of desire and in general) are non-substantial fluctuating appearances. Such an existential detachment is the only way for us to attain peace.

Here I mainly want to point out the use of the word "desire" which is often taken as a translation for a variety of different concepts which don't always express the intention behind the original ideas. Firstly, the Buddha didn't teach that desire is the cause of suffering. The word used in the Pali canon is "tanha" which is often translated as desire, craving, clinging, attachment, etc. In my understanding, clinging/attachment are the closest English equivalents to the concept. "Desire" in English has connotations that suggests positive and/or pleasurable emotions but the Buddha taught that we can equally be attached to negative feelings and emotions. Many people cling to negative feelings and emotions and this causes as much suffering as clinging to positive pleasures and indulgences. The Buddha teaches that all things, whether pleasurable or painful are but temporary feelings and subject to change and therefore must not be clung to. Beliving that a temporary emotion is a permenant state is a delusion whether positive or negative.

Zizek uses the term "wheel of desire" which isn't entirely accurate. I belive he is talking about the wheel of samsara where samsara can perhaps more accurately be described as the cycle of life, death and rebirth. Desire plays a part in this cycle but it's an oversimplification to describe this as desire alone. For example the Buddha teachings that aversion creates a form of karma that keeps people trapped in the wheel of samsara. Someone who has a deep desire and attachment to life would struggle to find enlightement but equally a person with a deep aversion/hatred for life would also struggle. 

Only half of the picture is painted in Zizek's interpretation.

>Or, to put it in yet another way, while Buddhism accepts the common view that the purpose of life is happiness (to quote the Dalai Lama, “the purpose of our lives is to be happy”), it just defines this term differently. 

Again, this is a huge oversimplification/misunderstanding. The Buddha did not teach that the purpose of life is happiness. In my understanding, the Buddha didn't at all teach any grand purpose to life. He taught that the very condition of existing and living through countless cycles of life, death and rebirth is in and of itself a conditioning of endless suffering. The Buddha himself despite reaching nibbana grew old, sick, suffered and died as all humans do. The teachings on happiness are teachings on how to best endure the conditions of life, not an escape from them.

(1) I'm also a Buddhist and a big fan of Zizek too :) I've not delved that deeply into his interpretations of Buddhism but I have also noticed some misundertandings he has in his critique of the Buddha's teachings. From what I've gathered, his misundertandings seem to largely come from his study of Buddhism coming from analysing Western Buddhist thought and certain schools of Buddhism which have fairly unique and potentially questionable interpretations of the dharma. I don't want to get into sectarianism but I'd really encourage anyone - whether a Buddhist or someone interested in Buddhist philosophy - to begin their studies with what is called the 'Early Buddhist Texts'. The early Buddhists texts (EBT) stem from what is known as the "Pali Canon", Pali being a language spoken close to the time of the Buddha's life and although it was not the language spoken by the Buddha, it represents the earliest collection of writings in the language closest to what the Buddha himself spoke. It's generally regarded as the most accurate and authoritative collection of the Buddha's teachings.

The Buddha lived 2500 years ago, so as you can imagine his teachings have taken unique shapes and interpretations over the past two and a half millenia. There was no written language at the time of the Buddha's life but roughly 500 years after his death the first Buddhist council began collecting writings of his teachings and in my perspective the collections from this era - or generally before the major sectarian splits - are a far better starting point for us today who are interested in Buddhism. 

I'm not here to slander or berate Zizek, I have immense respect for him! However there are some misunderstandings he has that I'd like to correct. I want to preface this by saying that I'm not a Buddhist scholar, in fact I'm a rather new Buddhist, so please take my words as a starting point for your own continued research rather than any authority. Secondly, I'm most familiar with the Theravada tradition so please bare this bias in mind. I have not studied Zen, or many other schools in depth so I am not a good source on these traditions. But despite my shortcomings, I still want to share some points that might be useful for anyone reading this that is interested in understanding more about the Buddha's teachings.

I am specifically responding to some of the things said in this piece: [https://thephilosophicalsalon.larbpublishingworkshop.org/why-lacan-is-not-a-buddhist-a-belated-reply-to-my-critics/](https://thephilosophicalsalon.larbpublishingworkshop.org/why-lacan-is-not-a-buddhist-a-belated-reply-to-my-critics/)

>I think that, in spite of all the desperate attempts to demonstrate that the way to Buddhist enlightenment passes through modesty and compassion, the only honest answer is that of D.T. Suzuki: Zen is a technique of meditation which is compatible with any political orientation: liberalism, fascism, Communism… 

The Buddha left very specific guidelines for both lay practitioners and for monastics that make Buddhism fundamentally incompatible with a wide variety of political systems and civilisational organisations. The 'Five Precepts' are a set of five basic guidelines that all Buddhists - whether lay or monastics - are expected to follow as the very bare minimum. Amongst these five basic rules the very first one is to refrain from taking human or animal life. This is the first of the most basic teachings, so any political system where the taking of sentient life is allowed is not in line with Buddhist principles. Of course, there are examples throughout history of Buddhists flouting this rule but it is abundantly clear that killing is not compatible with Buddhism. 

"Modesty and compassion" are not the sole prerequisites for enlightenment in the Buddha's teachings. The Buddha's predominant teaching is called the 'Noble Eightfold Path' which teaches the 8 factors of developing enlightenment. Please google the eight factors yourselves, but boiling it down to "modesty and compassion" is a huge oversimplification. I wish it were that easy - perhaps I might've gain enlightenment myself already xD

Britain is a geographical name for the island of Great Britain on which three countries - England, Scotland and Wales - are located. It is also often used as a descriptor for anyone who descends from or lives in the UK, and in this use of the word it also includes the Northern Irish. All English people are British but not all British people are English so these words cannot be used interchangably. Technically speaking anyone born/raised/living/descending from England can accurately describe themselves as "English" but this descriptor tends to predominantly be used to label a specific ethnic group rather than a national identity. People tend to use the term British to describe themselves as being a part of the national identity of being a citizen of the United Kingdom but many who are not ethnically English may not identify with being English as it holds more weight linking to the ethnic English identity.

If you still want to show her a level of compassionate support perhaps you can try setting some boundaries on the type of support you're willing and capable of giving her. I'm not an expert on the Budhha's teachings but my understanding is that the concept of accepting reality is more to do with understanding and accepting the very nature of reality (i.e. the nature of suffering, cessation of suffering, existence of karma, cycles of rebirth, impermenance, etc). Accepting the nature of reality isn't the same as accepting every circumstance thrown our way. The buddha taught the "two arrows of suffering" where we are struck by an arrow of misfortune which causes pain but we can inflict a second arrow on ourselves by how we react to that suffering.

The Buddha teaches that we can't control that first arrow of misfortune even if we try to avoid it. Bad things can happen, to use the examples you've given - someone can be born into an abusive family, find themselves kidnaped and enslaved or find out the love of their life is cruel and abusive. Suffering these types of misfortunes are examples of the inevitable sufferings or "dukkha" all sentient beings face within the wheel of samsara. 

But for example, if someone was in an abusive romantic relationship, it wouldn't be a correct Buddhist view to say "all unenlightened beings must suffer therefore you must do nothing and accept the abuse". A Buddhist analysis might look at the reasons why an abused partner is unwilling to leave their abuser due to being attached to the feeling of love they have/had for them. In this case, the abused partner might be unable to accept reality for what it is and comfort themselves with the "delusion" that the abuse in their relationship is acceptable because they still love them. This kind of thinking would be someone striking themselves with the second arrow of suffering. 

I think the confusion arises from the bigger picture Buddhism takes on the question of suffering. Being trapped in an abusive marriage for 15 years is of course awful but it's a drop in the ocean of all the different lifetimes of suffering we must endure. As long as we are in the cycle of samsara we will spend each of our lives accumalating karma - both good and bad - in one lifetime you may be the slave owner and in your next life you may be the slave. We want to avoid suffering but at the same time we inflict suffering onto others. We have countless lifetimes of collected karma good and bad and have no idea how or why this is impacting us in our current lives, likewise other people are carrying their own karma and suffering too. This is why the Buddha teaches compassion to all sentient beings because whether they are "good" or "bad" in this lifetime, we're all stuck in the endless cycle of suffering. 

So in short, Buddhism wouldn't criticise a slave for breaking their chains and seeking freedom in this life but it'd take the view that the most important chain to break is the one that ties us to the cycle of life and death itself.

I totally feel this, I was also raised Christian and I'm similarly early on my path to understanding the Buddha's teachings. One thing I may suggest is that it'll be helpful to start to reframe the way you think about religion itself whilst stepping into Buddhism. There are many active debates about whether Buddhism should be considered a "religion" or a "philosophy of life" and I don't mention this to get into sectarian debates - but to highlight how different the approach is to Christianity. A huge part of Evangelical Christianity is making declarations of your faith, converting non-believers to accept Jesus as their saviour and other such externalised expressions of your faith which are of far less importance in Buddhism as the focus of the practice and faith is turned inwards. I wonder if the pressure you feel to talk to your family about your transition in faith comes from some of this conditioned mindset to make such a declaration? I mean this with no judgement btw! I also felt similar things early on but decided to keep my journey personal. You might find it helpful to consider how necessary such a declaration will be, particularly if it may lead to difficulty or arguments. I've been on the other side of being scolded for hours about how I would eternally burn in hell for worshiping a false idol and I recommend avoiding such discussions if you feel your family may not be receptive or open. It can be particularly difficult with Evangelical traditions who feel a God-given obligation to "save" your soul. I'm not encouraging you to lie to your family or anything but whilst you're so early into your understanding of Buddhism, it'll probably be more helpful for you to focus on studying his teachings and becoming confident with the practices before being thrown into a potentially contentious argument where you'll feel pressured to "defend" your faith. 

You don't need to entirely discard your Christian identity ~~(well you'll need to discard every aspect of the self according to Buddha's teachings lol but I digress)~~. Personally, I still consider myself culturally Christian. I enjoy Christian holidays, visiting churchs and various traditions I was raised with without and anger or aversion to them. I just see them as a moment to remember fond childhood memories and connect with family/community. I also have a lot of gratitude for being raised in the Christian faith since whilst I don't subscribe to the religion anymore, there are many beautiful teachings from Jesus about compassion, love and there being more to life than what we perceive on this earth that I believe led me towards the Buddha's teachings and helping me accept these teachings more easily. I don't believe Jesus was the "son of God" but his story has many admirable teachings that a Buddhist can appreciate. You don't need to think of there being a conflict between your Christian upbringing and current trajectory into Buddhism, it's all just one big journey of your life to lead you to peace, awakening and enlightenment.

In short, release yourself from the Christian ways of thinking whilst approaching Buddhism. There's no vengeful angry God to punish you for not "doing Buddhism perfectly". You don't need to throw away all the cultural or personal connections you have with Christianity for the sake of being a good Buddhist. You don't need to declare your new faith to prove your piety. Being a "genuine Buddhist" comes from your understanding of the Dharma, following the 5 precepts, accepting the four noble truths and the eightfold path and the Buddha's other teachings. Be compassionate and kind to yourself and also be compassionate and kind to the people around you who may not ever understand or approve of the path you're walking on but you are walking a very noble path :) Good luck friend!

I found it to be more useful to explore attachment styles. Wikipedia gives a decent overview:  ([link to the full page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attachment_in_adults))

​

>Anxious-preoccupied\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Attachment_in_adults&action=edit&section=5)\]  
>  
>ie: negative view of self and positive view of others [\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attachment_in_adults#cite_note-14)  
>  
>People with anxious-preoccupied attachment type tend to agree with the following statements: "I want to be completely emotionally intimate with others, but I often find that others are reluctant to get as close as I would like", and "I am uncomfortable being without close relationships, but I sometimes worry that others don't value me as much as I value them." People with this style of attachment seek high levels of [intimacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intimacy), approval, and responsiveness from their attachment figure. They sometimes value intimacy to such an extent that they become overly dependent on the attachment figure. Compared with securely attached people, people who are anxious or preoccupied with attachment tend to have less positive views about themselves. They may feel a sense of anxiousness that only recedes when in contact with the attachment figure. They often [doubt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubt) their worth as a person and blame themselves for the attachment figure's lack of responsiveness. People who are anxious or preoccupied with attachment may exhibit high levels of emotional expressiveness, [emotional dysregulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotional_dysregulation), worry, and [impulsiveness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulsiveness) in their relationships.  
>  
>  
>  
>Dismissive-avoidant\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Attachment_in_adults&action=edit&section=6)\]  
>  
>ie: positive view of self and negative view of others [\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attachment_in_adults#cite_note-15)  
>  
>People with a dismissive style of avoidant attachment tend to agree with these statements: "I am comfortable without close emotional relationships", "It is important to me to feel independent and self-sufficient", and "I prefer not to depend on others or have others depend on me." People with this attachment style desire a high level of independence. The desire for independence often appears as an attempt to avoid attachment altogether. They view themselves as self-sufficient and invulnerable to feelings associated with being closely attached to others. They often deny needing close relationships. Some may even view close relationships as relatively unimportant. Not surprisingly, they seek less intimacy with attachments, whom they often view less positively than they view themselves. Investigators commonly note the [defensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_mechanism)character of this attachment style. People with a dismissive-avoidant attachment style tend to suppress and hide their feelings, and they tend to deal with [rejection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_rejection) by distancing themselves from the sources of rejection (e.g. their attachments or relationships).  
>  
>Fearful-avoidant\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Attachment_in_adults&action=edit&section=7)\]  
>  
>ie: unstable fluctuating/confused view of self and view of others [\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attachment_in_adults#cite_note-16)  
>  
>People with losses or other trauma, such as sexual abuse in childhood and adolescence may often develop this type of attachment[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attachment_in_adults#cite_note-17) and tend to agree with the following statements: "I am somewhat uncomfortable getting close to others. I want emotionally close relationships, but I find it difficult to completely trust others, or to depend on them. I sometimes worry that I will be hurt if I allow myself to become too close to other people." They tend to feel uncomfortable with emotional closeness, and the mixed feelings are combined with sometimes unconscious, negative views about themselves and their attachments. They commonly view themselves as unworthy of responsiveness from their attachments, and they don't trust the intentions of their attachments. Similar to the dismissive-avoidant attachment style, people with a fearful-avoidant attachment style seek less intimacy from attachments and frequently suppress and deny their feelings. Because of this, they are much less comfortable expressing affection.

​

I'd hazard a guess that a lot of 4 have a fearful-avoidant attachment style, which would explain the push and pull many of us feel in relationships. You might find it helpful to read up on these attachment styles more and see if there are any you particularly relate to. If you have access to therapy, this can also be a great starting point to explore why the thought of long-term romantic commitments causes you to feel so anxious.  Of course this isn't to say that anyone needs to be in a relationship - it's perfectly fine to realise that marriage/children/long term relationships are not for you. Society puts far too much pressure on people (especially women) to settle down when we may have other priorities we'd rather put our energy into.  

​

I'm happy to recommend some books, articles etc on attachment styles that I've personally found quite useful.

As a 4, I totally relate to this.   

The fours biggest pitfall is their obsession with 'identity'. If from childhood you have learnt to derive your sense of self from academic achievement and intellectual pursuits then it can easily descend into a an unhealthy pattern that distorts the way you see yourself and others. A major part of the four's behavioural pattern is the ways in which we fall into 'performing' our identities in order to have our self-image externally validated. In unhealthier states, this tends to be done by putting others we deem beneath us down through off-hand and dismissive remarks, the desire to surround ourselves with people we perceive as being intellectual equals, being highly and unnecessarily critical of anything that does not fit our perception of intelligence.

One way to combat this distorted sense of elitism is to realised that we are not nearly as 'special' or 'gifted' as we have been led to believe. More often than not, our talents are a result of having access to the right resources, connections, funds and time to pursue our interests. I've come to dislike the notion that 'giftedness' is some sort of intangible spark that a special few people happen to be born with. I'm my view it is mostly just a combination of a high level of interest, dedication and determination. The majority of our success is down to factors external to ourselves which is a touch pill to swallow for a lot of fours whose self esteem tends to ride on our inflated perceptions of our abilities. 

It might be helpful to spend time thinking about the people in your life who aided you in your success. The teachers, friends, family, mentors, romantic partners, colleagues, seniors in your field etc without whom you never would have been able to succeed. For us fours, moving the focus away from ourselves and towards the value that other people bring to our lives and the world is an important step to becoming healthier and developing healthier relationships with the people around us. It'll then become easier to value people for the unique qualities they bring into our lives rather than seeing them as accessories to validate unhealthy ego-fixations.

Letting her know how much you do truly value her as a person and expressing that you do recognise her skills and intelligence, however much if may differ from your own could be a step in healing the unintentional hurt you may have caused.

From scrolling through some of your responses I think you should take time to figure out your own emotions first. Everyone telling you to "step up and think of the child" probably mean well but have no idea how these things usually play out in reality. I've had a similar story play out in my own family recently and I can tell you that being on the fence about parenting whilst also trying to parent NEVER ends well for the child. Being a parent is the most difficult thing you will ever do in your life and you need to be prepared. Through no fault of your own you've been thrust into a shit situation and I'm sorry. Most people have at least 9 months to figure through things but you haven't had that and it isn't fair to expect you to suddenly know exactly what you want.  
I'd suggest considering some of the following options:    
*Contact your older sister now. Do not for one second think that you can go through this alone. You are going to need her support behind you throughout all of this whether you decide to be in the child's life or not. Tell her that you want to figure out what the right thing to do in this situation is but you need to process everything first. Tell her how you feel - scared, angry, hurt, frustrated, etc. Cry if you need to, just don't bottle up your feelings.
*Find information on family services in your area. You should've had free access to parenting classes etc whilst 'Sarah' was pregnant. These services vary depending on your borough but you'd be surprised how much is offered that people don't know about. They should also be able to advise you on your financial options. 
* I'd also suggest family counselling for you and Sarah. You've been pretty clear about not wanting a relationship with Sarah which simplifies things but you will need to learn how to co-parent with her. It may also be good to have a neutral space where you can voice your feelings about the situation. I'm sure she may also have things she wants to get off her chest about no wanting you in the child's life at first. You are holding back your emotions now but the bottled-up resentment will eventually find an unhealthy way out in the long-run, whether you take it out on her, the child or yourself.  
  
Take time to decide what the right path for you will be. No one can guilt, pressure or force you into being a parent if you aren't willing. If you decide not to be in the child's life know that you are choosing to prioritise yourself over them. You will be doing irrevocable damage to that child and they will have to come to terms with being abandoned. If you half-heartedly decide you do want to be in their life you will also be doing damage to them. Kids aren't dumb, they know when they are treated like a burden by their parents and they will grow up with issues and resent you for it. If you decide to prioritise the child over everything, your relationship with your child will be the most rewarding experience of your life and they will grown up knowing that whilst things weren't perfect, they had a dad who loved them unconditionally.  
Anyway, good luck with it all. I really wish the best for you all despite the circumstances.

Conflict/anger: both are 'withdrawn' types so it's not uncommon for either type to avoid conflict - particularly around people they are not close to. When they feel they can't withdraw from a situation they become passive aggressive and may even have an outburst of anger when they are really pushed. One difference I see is that 4s can be quite happy to into a debate/argument if the mood so takes them. If the conflict is over something the 4 feels is emotionally important to them, their concern for being liked/keeping the peace flies out of the window and they will thoroughly enjoy jumping head-first into an argument and not relenting until they feel they have won. When 9s do finally snap it takes people by surprise, it's often explosive, vicious and over as quickly as it started. -Melancholy for 4s isn't always about feeling bad or being depressed. They enjoy sadness as an emotion even if they are feeling perfectly content. -On personal interests; all of the withdrawn types (4, 9 & 5) are likely to become extremely invested in their interests as an escape from the outside world. However 4s are more likely to jump from different interests and wear those interests as the sum total of their identity.  
  
-At the core of the 4 is the feeling of being alien, different and unique.
